utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go back to the previous question, you mentioned Andrew Purvis, the representative of Time magazine.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andrew Purvis is the head of the department for Central Europe for Time magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that, with Purvis, on the 15th of July this year, while you were a witness here and giving statements, that you were in the Freedom Association, or rather, the National Committee for my defence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, why did you represent yourself as being an interpreter at the time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was technically what I was at that particular time. Mr. Purvis was doing his journalist assignment, and I was just there to translate and interpret for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that it was proper conduct, in view of the fact that you were already a witness here, to represent yourself under false pretensions there and to introduce yourself as being an interpreter to the people working in the committee on my defence?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I did. I did not introduce myself under false pretensions. I said I was a journalist but I was working as an interpreter at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Anastasijevic. Now, tell me this: With respect to the incident that took place in Tuzla in the summer of 1992, are you quite certain that you explained that whole incident to us as it happened?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have any more questions to ask, I said that I wrote an article, a report, ten years ago. I wasn't able to go through the whole article and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a journalist, did you attend any combat operation undertaken by the JNA from the time that you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat operation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said here that the JNA was not in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the JNA was not in the town itself or that there was no great JNA presence there, but the JNA was situated around the town and used the artillery with respect to the siege of the town and the attack on the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you say that the JNA gave logistic support to some kind of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of everything I was able to see during my stay in Vukovar and its environs at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of logistic support did you see there?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that the so-called volunteer units were using weapons which in normal times were only used by the JNA and its units, and it was logical to assume that they had received it from the JNA itself. And also about the 20th of November, 1991, I happened to see guns, cannons, belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army attacking in the direction of the town, and at that time the Serb forces were taking control of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Serb forces. Do you mean the Serbs who lived in Vukovar and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking about the JNA reservists, the volunteer units, and the members of the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as you know, those are people who actually live in the area. They are locals.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they might be members of the Territorial Defence, but at their head was a man by the name of Radovan Stojicic. He is no longer living, but he is not from that area. And as far as volunteers are concerned, they mostly came from Serbia, the majority of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the events that took place in Vukovar and the several months during which the Serb citizens were taken away, killed, investigations taken, initiated, they were detained, and everything that led to the conflicts in that area? And I mean Vukovar and the surrounding parts when I say that.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was happening to the Serb population I learnt from some of them quite a lot later, and that predominantly from the Croatian press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the Croatian press, you say.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian papers, the Feral Tribune wrote extensively about the activities of Tomislav Mercep who, at that time, was a functionary in Vukovar and whose unit had abused the Serbs and taken them away. And I got the first information about that from the Croatian paper, the Feral Tribune.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you were in Vukovar at the time, you talked to no one, you heard nothing about the killings, the arrests and all the other things that took place - how shall I put it? - all the other acts of violence, to put it very mildly, vis-a-vis the Serb population there in Vukovar and its environs and settlements around it.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a lot of stories and rumours going round. Some of them were quite unbelievable, others I couldn't check out at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that the Serb villages were completely under -- undamaged and the Croatian ones completely damaged.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said mostly completely undamaged and mostly completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that Mercep and his fighters who had killed so many people, Serb civilians over there, were not engaged in destruction of any kind in those villages.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life have I seen Tomislav Mercep, nor did I talk to him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that movement around the region of Eastern Slavonia was very dangerous at that time because the Croatian snipers were there and were active from the pockets, as you call them, in which they were located.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From which positions did these snipers open fire along the positions of these territorial members?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Vukovar, they were shooting from Borovo Naselje settlement and a part of town called Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear at that time about how many civilians and soldiers were killed from these activities of theirs, these onslaughts?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible to get exact figures at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said here that you conducted an interview with Goran Hadzic five or six days after the fall of Vukovar, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand all this correctly, or if I did, it wasn't actually an interview, it was a press conference; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a press conference after which Goran Hadzic -- that is to say, after the press conference, he talked to journalists individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that some 15 journalists were present on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that on that occasion, he was fairly critically disposed or very critically disposed towards the JNA. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that the JNA gave logistic support to those units. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, does that seem to you to be illogical or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came to understand at that time that we -- there were political talks between Goran Hadzic and the authorities of SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and the top military echelon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, Mr. Anastasijevic, in 1999, you left Yugoslavia in the month of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were a military conscript, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to leave the country then?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By bus, via Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you consider that, as a military conscript, you were free to leave the country during the NATO pact aggression?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that once you left the country in the period between -- that is to say when you left and up until you returned, that you spent your time in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you make a livelihood while you were in Vienna? How were you able to make ends meet?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the bureau of Time magazine for Central Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Anastasijevic, did you ever conduct any investigations and research for any kind of Western house with respect to violations of the oil embargo on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did write some texts and articles on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a particular report, reportage, I think it was in 1996 or 1997, on the contraband of cigarettes and smuggling of cigarettes and oil from Montenegro. And I remember one of these articles that I was engaged in in 1994 with respect to the blockade of the Danube and how oil was being smuggled against that -- across the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you received money for taking foreigners to see where the oil embargo was being violated, where the FRY were violating the oil embargo?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as a local producer for an Italian television crew, and in that capacity, I was paid a fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said how you had interviews with Raznjatovic, nicknamed Arkan, and that he criticised the JNA too and said that the JNA was not defending the Serbs. I understood you to say that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that he wasn't defending them sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion; as far as I understood you, he refused all assertions -- he denied all assertions that the members of his volunteer units took part in any war crimes whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a special operations unit as well. Have you ever seen a special operations unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Croatia at all?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the time you are talking about, no special operations units were in existence at all?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to 1991, then at that time, 1992, there were a lot of units that were called the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you said that you didn't see them in Bosnia or anywhere else, these Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them personally, but I met him people who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you know anything about the activities of the leaders in Vukovar, those people who called themselves the Ustashas? That's how they referred to one another. And Mercep was among them. Blago Zadro, Mirko Dragicevic, Jure Marusic, Branislav Glavas, all those names; have you heard of them? Mirko Glavas, Ante Budimir, et cetera? People who had organised themselves as far back as the beginning of March, 1991, in the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt of these names and heard about them much later, mostly from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what conclusions they had already brought in on the 10th of March, 1991? I mean the conclusions that they adopted according to which all Serbs should be dismissed from their jobs in the state administration, in the police force, et cetera, and that pressure should be brought to bear against them to leave the area, and where pressure wasn't working, then more drastic measures should be adopted, such as arrests, killings, and so on. As a journalist dealing with matters of this kind and that area, did you know anything about that at the time or did you learn of it later?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of it later from the information media. I learnt of some details. But at that time, I was not aware of the details. I didn't know about them with respect to the functioning of the Croatian authorities in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you link up what was going on at that time with the resistance that the Serbs set up to those authorities?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a journalist, I wrote articles and reported on what I saw happening in the field on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said a moment ago that you saw no JNA operation taking place, either in Bosnia or in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw a JNA operation around Vukovar and in Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you stated here that you were not present when anybody fell casualty, that you didn't see anybody kill anybody at that particular time, and that you did not see personally, yourself, any kind of violence taking place. So you moved around the area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that nobody had killed anybody in front of my own eyes, but I also said that I saw many signs that crimes were being perpetrated. For example, I remember very well I saw a soldier who just had a bloody machete of weapons, and when I asked him where his rifle was, he said he didn't need a rifle because the weapon he had with him was quite sufficient for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you conclude from this, from hearing what he said, that he was going around slaughtering people with that machete; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my reporting, I just conveyed what I saw and I left the readers to make their own conclusions, having read the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in the war in Croatia, the state security gave military and logistic support through Mihalj Kertes, Stanisic, Brana Crncevic. You say that Brana Crncevic procured weapons. Do you know that he's a writer, that he was not involved in such things? And were you ever present when any such thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer about that man you mentioned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to being a writer, as he still is, at that time, Brana Crncevic was head of Matica Srpska, which was registered as a humanitarian organisation, and he was often in Croatia and Bosnia in this connection. However, I also know that that humanitarian organisation did not only distribute humanitarian aid; cars were also involved. There was a lot of talk going around in those days that weapons were being distributed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how old an organisation Matica Srpska is?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it dates back to the nineteenth century, but I don't see what that has to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a writer, president of Matica Srpska, and now you say that you heard that they were distributing weapons. Are you just presenting hearsay here, rumours you heard from someone that Matica Srpska was distributing weapons?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from someone that Brana Crncevic, taking advantage of his position in Matica Srpska, was distributing weapons. Yes, that is what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from, please? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from persons whose names I would not wish to mention at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you are giving claims that are very serious. You say that you heard from some people, and you don't want to give their names. How is this possible, actually? How is it possible to check such information, then?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mention Veselin Sljivancanin. Did you see one single crime that Sljivancanin committed, or did you hear that he ordered any crime to be committed? Did you know anything about that? Did you know of any crime?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that. I did not see my -- Major Sljivancanin at that time committing any crime, but subsequently I heard, like many people, what happened at the Ovcara farm where over 200 persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the involvement of the JNA in that which happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was involved from the JNA in that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Veselin Sljivancanin who, at that time, headed the 1st Motorised Brigade. He allowed members of the so-called Territorial Defence to kill the people who were taken out of the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what can you claim that he allowed them to kill them?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the fact that these people were taken out of the hospital in Vukovar by soldiers who were under the command of Major Sljivancanin, and on the basis of the fact that these persons were subsequently found dead. That is to say that they were either killed by JNA soldiers, which is probably not true, or, as I heard from many sources, that they were killed by persons from the Territorial Defence of Eastern Slavonia after the Yugoslav People's Army or, rather, Sljivancanin handed them over to them, to the Territorial Defence, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you've been saying, it means that they practically lost their lives in that local conflict, and you do not have any proof of Sljivancanin having handed them over. You simply infer this on the basis of the fact that some of them were taken away by soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I infer that not only be the basis of that but also on the basis of very detailed stories I heard from persons who at that time were within the JNA and whose names are well known to the Tribunal because these names are contained in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just clarify this. You are talking about all of this as a journalist. You are talking about stories you heard from various persons who were moving about that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you personally did not see or hear any of the things that you are talking about except for these stories of these alleged eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean what I am asking you about; the role of the JNA, Sljivancanin, and so on.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please formulate these questions more specifically. I saw certain things with my very own eyes, and I heard about others from others. It cannot be put that way, that I did not see anything and that I wrote everything down only on the basis of what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Finally, what did you see in relation to Sljivancanin, everything that you are accusing him of and the JNA? What did you see specifically?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Major Veselin Sljivancanin in Ovcara at the time. Everything I said in relation to Ovcara then was indeed obtained from statements made by persons that I talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that happened in Eastern Slavonia, and according to the claims that you made, that is part of these local forces. What does this have to do with Serbia? Would you tell me that.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it has to do with the Yugoslav People's Army, I didn't say it had to do with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You explain that there was not enough room in prisons and that the army opened camps in Serbia. Is this some assumption of yours? Could you please tell me where was a camp ever opened in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two camps were opened. One in the village of Stajicevo and the other in Begejci; that is to say both in Vojvodina. These were camps for prisoners of war from Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. You are saying that when the army took people prisoner, that they held them in some centre of theirs; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the prisoner of war from Eastern Slavonia were taken to three places; one was the prison in Mitrovica where part of the prison was put under JNA control, and the remaining two places I mentioned are the ones that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the JNA do to these prisoners of war, as you say? How long did they keep them there? What did they do to them?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept them there until the agreement was signed with Croatia sometime at the beginning of 1992 about the exchange of prisoners, and these people who were then in the territory of the Republic of Serbia were exchanged or, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For imprisoned soldiers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any violence committed against them in those facilities where they were kept as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they treated in accordance with -- in accordance with the way a civilised army, as the JNA was, was to be expected to behave?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that everything in relation to the events in Ovcara that you've been referring to was handed over to the military prosecutor and that it was the military authorities that were supposed to establish responsibility in this respect?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that some investigation was being carried out, but I never saw the ultimate findings of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you not interested in seeing what the investigation would establish?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was interested, but I simply never managed to get a hold of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. Our time is very short. Please. Your claim concerning Seselj, that he organised volunteers at the request of Jovica Stanisic, how did you come up with that claim?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This claim comes from Vojislav Seselj himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where and when did he make this claim to you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party in the street called Francuska in Belgrade, sometime in 1994. I can't remember exactly what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a recording of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not record the conversation, I took notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He claims, for example, that he never said that to you and that this is an absolute fabrication, which is, of course, what I had assumed.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of Mr. Seselj having denied this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know that a vast number of articles were published about all sorts of things over these past ten years in various newspapers and magazines, and people didn't feel it necessary to deny 90 per cent of what was written there because people thought there was no need to do that. What does it mean that he never denied it? Does that mean that he confirms it if he never denied it? For example, do you know that I personally never denied anything and that for ten years there was not a single newspaper that didn't write something against me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going some way from the point. The witness says Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that he doesn't know that Mr. Seselj has ever denied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, you are testifying about things that you heard of. You're a journalist. Tell me, was there freedom of press in Yugoslavia over those ten years?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not put it that way, that there was freedom of press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were the constraints on the press? Do you know how many newspapers there were, radio stations, TV stations; big ones, small ones, local ones, nation-wide ones, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that your government had under very firm control media like the national television and major daily newspapers, whereas a small number of media that had a very limited circulation or a very limited range, as far as electronic media are concerned, were allowed to operate more or less freely, but these were very small media that certainly could not reach the wider public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Couldn't Studio B reach the wider public? Or Blic, for example, or your magazine Vreme; all these papers? There were a couple of thousand newspapers and weekly magazines in Serbia and an enormous number of electronic media, local media and so on. Did anybody restrict that in any way?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were various restrictions, institutional and non-institutional. Those media that could significantly affect the public opinion, that is to say that had a large circulation or a wide range, were under government control, whereas the other ones, the small ones were there as a kind of alibi so that people could say that there was freedom of press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But was any newspaper banned over those ten years?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Open bans were rarely applied. But, for example, the daily newspaper Borba was taken over by the government, by a provisional ruling of a court. Studio B was put understate control a few times. And now that we are on this subject, yes, I remember that on the 9th of March, Studio B was closed and the police broke into its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the day when they were inciting violence. Do you think that that is the right of journalists, to incite to violence?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that journalists should incite violence, but I don't remember that that is what Studio B was doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, which were these newspapers that were firmly in the control of government?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Politika, Politika Ekspres, Vecernje Novosti.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say Borba too, because Borba is a state newspaper?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borba was partly within the federal -- beg your pardon, under the federal government in terms of being owned by the federal government, but it pursued an independent editorial policy. However, that cannot be said about Political, Politika Ekspres, or Vecernje Novosti during your rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said just now that Borba was partly owned by the federal government. How come then, if it is owned by the federal government and if the federal government appointed the director of Borba, do you consider that to be a takeover the Borba?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was some kind of a court ruling but I'm not really an expert in ownership matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not take go into all of that then, but let's take Politika, Politika Ekspres, and Vecernje Novosti, the newspapers you referred to. Do you know, for example, that in that period of time from 1990 until 2000, in these newspapers only, Politika, Politika Ekspres - to the least extent in Politika but in Vecernje Novosti too - how many hundreds of articles were published against me?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these newspapers during your rule, I do not remember having read a single article that would be critical of your rule and your government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Anastasijevic, as a journalist, why didn't you look at their archives and then you will see this story about a state media, what the situation actually was. But we don't have time for that now. I see that time is flying. Tell me, so you claim that there was not a single article of this kind. Fine. This is a very good statement, a very useful statement. You explained that you were in Foca when you described the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Foca, the army of Yugoslavia was not in Foca at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was not there, right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the army of Yugoslavia was not in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that at that time, those units were not there either, those units that you mentioned, the units of Vuk Draskovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units were in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that at that time, as far as I can remember, I don't know if you can remember, this person Lainovic that you refer to, that he disassociated himself from Vuk Draskovic. He said he had nothing to do with Vuk Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this in my statement and I repeat it now: That in Foca in 1992, I saw members of the Serbian guard, a paramilitary organisation, an organisation of volunteers, that for a while was linked to Mr. Draskovic's party. That's what I said in my statement and that's what I'm repeating now. As for political relations at that time between Lainovic and Draskovic, I did not go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you are linking this to the party of Vuk Draskovic, was the party of Vuk Draskovic in opposition all the time? Was it against the authorities in Serbia? Were they not organising demonstrations and all the rest? Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the time, but for the most part, yes, because for a while, Mr. Draskovic was minister in your government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, 1999. And until 1999?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1999, this party was in opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does this have to do with anything, then, what you've been saying? What does this have to do with this indictment?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what various parts of my statement have to do with the indictment. You have to ask somebody else about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Anastasijevic, you were in Foca only for two days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During that time, you did not see any crimes. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I did not see any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You even say that there was not a curfew in place then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come you say that some 40 Muslims were detained or arrested? Have you seen this personally?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard it then from a man who at the time was at the head of the Crisis Staff. So he showed me the list with the names of these 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, you go to say that there was some forester who was in power then. What does Serbia have to do with forester in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man with the nickname Sumar, whose name I actually can't remember right now, was an organiser, and in his restaurant, headquarters of Serbian guard was established with the people who mostly came from Serbia and from Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these are the people from this opposition party that you just mentioned; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the army of Republika Srpska was a branch of the army of Yugoslavia. How did you come up with this idea? And don't you know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the army of Yugoslavia had absolutely no influence whatsoever over the command in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the army of Republika Srpska could be considered. I didn't claim that they were formally a part of the army of Yugoslavia, but factually they were. And I based this claim of mine on the fact that they paid out pensions, that the pensions for the officers of the army of Republika Srpska was paid out of Belgrade and that they actively were involved in supplying arms and participating occasionally in armed operations during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The economic aid to Republika Srpska in general is not contentious here, but don't you know that the army of Republika Srpska had its own command and that it had absolutely no command or disciplinary or any other link or connection with the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the army of Republika Srpska did not have the same treasury with them, but I never said that they received commands -- their commands from Belgrade, or orders from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you link this, whether you do it directly or not, but when you link these two things, then it creates an impression that they were part of the JNA, which is not true. Now, tell me this, please: You say that the weapons were -- arrived from Yugoslavia. Do you know that in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the time of former Yugoslavia, in view of the concept of national defence and in view of the central position geographically of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that for that very reason, in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was the greatest number of weapons, warehouses, and military manufacturing facilities? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it was located in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no need, therefore, to send weapons to Bosnia and Herzegovina; there were weapons there already. So they simply had to take hold of those depots of weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. There was a need to send spare parts and ammunition and occasionally personnel. And I saw with my own eyes that the JNA actively participated in 1994 with their artillery from which they fired from Serbia in the direction of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify that. I heard you say that before, and that is completely not true. Do you know that Yugoslavia lodged a protest to the Security Council because some shells landed on its territory? Yugoslavia never fired from its territory in the direction of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How did you come up with this?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came up with this because I saw these guns with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the guns, cannons, firing across the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time I was passing by, they weren't shooting but I saw empty cases lying around which indicated there had been shooting recently. And then I heard from people who lived in Serbia, on that part of the river, that they couldn't sleep all night because there were guns firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was during that battle in Gorazde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you heard from people that they were unable to sleep, do you know that the Drina River is some 100 to 150 metres wide in that place and that Gorazde is located on the Drina River and that if there are guns firing some 100 or 200 metres away from you, that you would have no trouble sleeping?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say that they had trouble sleeping because of the guns in Bosnia. They said that what caused problem for them were the guns that were located in Serbia along the road near the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, any kind of positioning of troops in Yugoslavia was done just in order to protect, to defend Yugoslavia, and this is the first time that I'm hearing that somebody was firing from Yugoslavia towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. You didn't see the guns firing, but you're claiming that you heard from the villagers that they were unable to sleep at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said this is what he saw with his own eyes. Now, there's no point going on about it as to what the villagers did or didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't see a single shell being fired from Yugoslavia towards Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Isn't that precisely what you said you did see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, let me just add this personnel factor: You said that the officers came to Republika Srpska from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, the JNA existed in the entire territory of Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did the officers come to the -- from to the Croat army and the Muslim army if not from the JNA? And I'm not here speaking about Mujahedin and the mercenaries that had arrived from various organisations such as Al Qaeda and others. I'm now referring to the officers of Yugoslav origin. Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're asking me about the officers in the Croatian army and the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, in view of the fact that all officers who existed in the former Yugoslavia were the officers of the JNA in 1991; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those who were in the JNA were in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, there was nobody who could send them to Croatian army, or Muslim Federation, as they called it at that time. There was nobody -- nobody had to do it. Those officers who were from those areas of Yugoslavia became officers in those armies, and that applied to everybody; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't apply to everyone, and things are not as simple as you're trying to portray them, but could you give me a specific question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, those officers, including those who were in the Croatian armed forces and those who were in the army of Republika Srpska and those that were in Muslim formations, excluding Mujahedin and others that came from outside, were also officers of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether some officers in the Croatian army or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina used to be formerly members of the JNA, then my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then why do you distinguish the officers of the army of Republika Srpska that also used to belong to the JNA and then later on became officers of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because all officers that originated from Bosnia and were of Serb ethnicity and were officers of the JNA, they had to transfer in 1992 to the army of Republika Srpska. There wasn't a single one who practically remained in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not true, Mr. Anastasijevic, that none of them remained in the JNA. Those who had Serbian or Montenegrin citizenship definitely were given an opportunity to remain in the army of Yugoslavia. And as far as the officers of Republika Srpska are concerned, do you think that somebody from Yugoslavia had ordered them to go to Bosnia, or perhaps they themselves wanted to remain there and to defend their villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed that I saw an order, I saw somebody ordering them this. All I said was that I saw that they, in an organised way, transferred to the VRS from VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that while the JNA still existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was one single military district in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that at the time the JNA still existed, General Mladic was the commander of that military district? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then once they seceded and the civil war broke out, they established the VRS, which is quite logical because the Muslims had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. established their own army, and Croatia made an incursion across the Sava River into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and started destructing areas there. Do you remember Sijekovac and Brod and other areas that were affected?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was your actual question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, do you know how many Muslims there were in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were several thousands of Muslims in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were entire brigades consisting of Muslims fighting in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point. He says he doesn't know how many there were. His point -- his evidence was on a very narrow point, which was to do with the officers being transferred. That's what he dealt with. You've got about ten minutes -- slightly more than ten minutes, but not much more, left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to saying that you don't know that somebody had issued this order to them but you assume that somebody had ordered them to transfer to the VRS, and then you also go on to list a number of reasons, but you omitted to mention patriotism and the fact that those people went to defend their homes and people who, as you know, numbered 2 million. There were 2 million Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that they went there pursuant to an order or they went there because they believed they had to defend from the aggression or, rather, from the violence that was committed against the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in my statement is something I will repeat now too. The officers who wished to continue their professional career in the military - and I'm not going to go into their personal motives now, so -- and those who were of Serb ethnicity and originated from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if they wished to continue their military career and remain in the army, they had to transfer from the JNA to the VRS. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Do you have any evidence to support this, that somebody had to transfer because he was ordered from the JNA to transfer to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have statements of a number of officers who at the time transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't transfer because they wanted to defend the people there but because somebody from Belgrade had ordered them. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that they had to go there because, as professional officers, they had to continue their career. This is what they used to say to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste any more time on this. You say that the border was closed, that that was in 1994. However, that one could pass through freely and that the weapons and ammunitions crossed the border freely. Why was the border closed at the time? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border was not formally closed for any kind of traffic. It was closed within the framework of economic sanctions that you imposed against Republika Srpska due to political conflict with Radovan Karadzic. Therefore, the border was closed for the traffic of goods; it didn't apply to military transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what was this political conflict all about?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, Radovan Karadzic refused to sign a peace plan that you supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this plan is actually known as Vance-Owen Plan and that was in 1993, not 1994, Mr. Anastasijevic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of peace plans, and I can't remember now exactly whether that was Vance-Owen's Plan or Owen-Stoltenberg. All I know is in August of 1994, conflict broke out between you and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Anastasijevic, this plan was in place in 1993. So this disagreement appeared in 1993, not in 1994. And this is when the blockade ensued. But do you know that Radovan Karadzic did sign that plan in the -- in Athens on May 1, 1993, in the presence of Cyrus Vance and David Owen and Greek Prime Minister Mitzotakis and other representatives of Greece and international community? He did sign that plan. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we're getting some way from this witness's evidence now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this witness doesn't even know when the Vance-Owen Plan was discussed due to which a conflict broke out between us and the leadership of Republika Srpska, and he's claiming something that's not true. These facts are well known to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's barely relevant to these proceedings what he knew or didn't know and whether he can give a date for things or not. Now, let's move on to something which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, this witness is giving evidence about things that are much less known than these generally known facts, and as far as the generally known facts are concerned, he's demonstrating that he knows nothing of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a general knowledge test. Now, he's giving evidence about specific things. Now, have you got anything more you want to ask him, anything more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He, in his statement, said that due to a blockade in 1994, which followed the conflict that broke out regarding the peace plan, this is something that's not true. This peace plan was in 1993, and the blockade was in that year. And it's not true that Karadzic did not sign it. He did sign it, but the Assembly of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made your point. As I said, it's not a general knowledge test. Now, have you any questions about his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that a Bosnian Serb who worked in the state security said that he had been send to Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that, as you say yourself, he was a Serb from Bosnia, a Bosnian Serb, and Velika Kladusa is in Bosnia-Herzegovina also? So do you allow for a possibility that he went there as a volunteer or perhaps he had there business of his own? Who sent him there, the state security from Serbia, or you have something else in mind? Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He claimed that he wasn't alone there. He was there with a number of other people that had worked for the police of Republika Srpska and that he had been sent there pursuant to an order from the MUP of Republika Srpska. What I thought was important in that story was that he and his people had insignia of the Fikret Abdic's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Fikret Abdic's people and Karadzic signed a peace plan and there were 98 per cent majority of Muslims in that area and they had no trouble moving about Republika Srpska freely, working, engaging in commerce there, and they signed a peace plan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Karadzic and Abdic had a very good relationship for a time. I know Fikret Abdic left. I saw him myself leaving the building of the government there. And you know yourself this because you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had a very good relationship with him yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a good working relationship with him, and I supported every kind of cooperation with him because he wanted to secure a good life and good economic activity for people in that area. I know in Krajina, I know that he tried to revive the farms and agriculture in that area, and I thought it was a good idea to have peace established at least in one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is there something wrong with that, Mr. Anastasijevic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I thought was particularly interesting there is that this member of the MUP of Republika Srpska fought in somebody else's army, in somebody else's uniform. Therefore, he did not have the insignia of the MUP of Republika Srpska or the army of Republika Srpska but he had insignia of the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia, and that was quite interesting for me. And as for the political cooperation between you or Karadzic with Abdic, this is something I cannot give comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you know that some people from Republika Srpska who might have been volunteers -- for example, perhaps they had relatives over there. As you know, there were many mixed marriages at the time, et cetera. So how do you know that he was sent by the MUP of Republika Srpska to go to Kladusa and fight there? Where do you get this idea from?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said he was ordered to do so, that is to say, to go there with his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what he told you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's the man's name?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have his name among my notes, but I can't recall it at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just let me have a look at my own notes here. You talked about and explained how Seselj told you that Stanisic had asked him what he did, and he said that is pure fabrication. Now, do you know what the relationships were between Stanisic and Seselj? Do you know that Seselj, on several occasions, was arrested, taken into custody as someone who was the president and present president of the Serbian Radical Party and that the interview that you are talking about, he gave to you when he came out of prison in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those relationships with Stanisic and sending volunteers to the battlefront, he didn't tell that to me. He said it to many other journalists on numerous other occasions. And I'm quite sure, although at that time I didn't have a camera because I'm working for the press, that you would be able to find audio and television recordings of the statements made by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that once he came out of prison in Gnjilane in 1995, that he had an interview with you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the interviews I conducted with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you then assume that he cooperated with the people who had put him in prison?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period in which Mr. Seselj claims that he did cooperate with Mr. Stanisic was the period of 1991, 1992, and 1993, not the period when there was a political clash between yourself and him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was well known that Seselj was in the opposition up until 1997.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that he was officially an opposition member, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Anastasijevic, I think you have just thought up what you say Seselj said. And you haven't got a tape or recording, although you all have the small tape recorders when you conduct interviews except you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Some people take notes, others like to make recordings. I myself prefer taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you think a politician can say, for example, in a political campaign that he is waging; that he's going to say things that are correct and things that are not correct or only things that are true and correct? What is your experience as a journalist? What do politicians tend to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a general question which is not going to assist the Trial Chamber. Mr. Milosevic, your last two questions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two questions? Only two more? That's very interesting. It's very difficult for me to make a selection now, Mr. May, but as this witness, fifth-hand witness is not a very significant one, it doesn't really matter. It's not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There too we're getting comments, Mr. Milosevic. We'll consider what the significance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, you said that there were policemen from Serbia in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I understood you to say that even you yourself say that they did not take part in any combat operations; right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of what people told me. They told me they hadn't taken part in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Is it logical or were you interested in finding out, if you met a policeman over there, that the job of the police force was to fight against criminals and that police forces cooperated in the struggle against crime, the police force of Serbia and of Republika Srpska in the struggle against crime, smuggling, unlawful dealings, and other criminal acts or, rather, the very fact that there was a war going on over there contributed largely to the increase of crime generally speaking? So did the -- did it ever occur to you that they were cooperating in this struggle against crime and that that was in the interests of all the citizens; Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and anybody else?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said was that there were exchanges of cadres and staff during the war between the MUP of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbia. That is to say that policemen went from Serbia to Bosnia and vice versa, that they went from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it logical that the police force of two neighbouring countries -- police forces of two neighbouring countries cooperate amongst themselves in that basic job of theirs, which is the struggle against crime? Does that seem to you to be logical?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of the details of the arrangement that the MUP of Republika Srpska had with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. All I said was what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If it's my last question, can we agree over this point, Mr. Anastasijevic: That you are not testifying here about anything you have actually seen but only about what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot agree on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't expect you to agree either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Anastasijevic, as you were in Vukovar, as you yourself stated, I should first of all like to ask you something with respect to what you happened to notice there. In your interviews and also in your statement, you said that you know that a meeting was held between the representatives of the local authorities and the representative of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at that meeting an agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct that the agreement was the following: That the soldiers, Croatian soldiers taken prisoner, they would be cared for and seen to by the territorial authorities, whereas the people who were taken prisoner, the Croatian soldiers who were in prisons in Serbia, that they would be taken over and cared for by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that what happened in Ovcara only took place after that agreement came into being?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that you heard one version of all that from a high-ranking military representative of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was about the fact that the army had handed over to the members of the Territorial Defence, led at the time by Radovan Stojicic, nicknamed Badza, these detainees on the factory farm of Ovcara, and allegedly it was said that they would be tried before the judicial organs of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Eastern Srem [as interpreted]. However, they were not taken to court there but what happened was that they were killed as soon as they were taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The representative of the JNA at that time, was he Colonel Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the 1st Motorised Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the first question I had for you. Now, moving on to another topic: As far as I was able to understand - I wasn't here when you were examined and questioned - but reading what -- your statement, you testified on -- basically on the basis of interviews that you had with individuals and the stories you heard from them and then, finally, on the basis of what you yourself saw; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this ten-year time period when you attended all these events, because you followed events in Bosnia and Croatia and in Kosovo as well, you were able to build up an opinion of your own, were you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have opinions on different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But was any particular opinion of yours dominant?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask me --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. I'm not insisting on that point. But when you went in the field, did you have a journalist's assignment?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you act within that journalist's assignment?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your texts, articles, in the interviews you had with various people, did you deal principally with problems that emerged from the centralisation of power and authority in Serbia and the taking away of the autonomy of provinces? Autonomy, I mean here with respect to the right of veto as well?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're talking about is highfalutin politics. What I delved in was reporting from the field, from the spot, on location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement here, we see this to be dominant, that is to say that all the problems and issues you brought up before the Prosecution, you say that they were the result of what was done in Serbia, where autonomy was taken away.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see -- say -- I don't know that I said anything along those lines with those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your articles and the interviews you had with the people you talked to, did you look into the consequences that could result if the republics were to secede and the state wither away?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was among the topics that I did discuss, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in one particular point in this regard, and I think you wrote about this in your articles, that the Ministry of Defence was created in Slovenia and Croatia much before they had actually proclaimed their independence.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How much time before this proclamation of independence?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember. Several months, perhaps a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know why Ministries of Defence are set up generally before a country is proclaimed independent under conditions in which there is no war yet?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Ministry of Defence is something that Serbia had in 1991 as well, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. That's precisely what I wanted to ask you. Now the Ministry of Defence, as you described it, was founded later on, after the previous two ministries; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I freely admit that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to move on to one other topic: You also wrote extensively about different problems. Now, in your articles, did you highlight the problem which existed in the minds of people not to have history repeat itself, or was that just sort of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be clearer? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This fear that people could fall victim, that they could lose their lives for no reason that existed in previous times, many people were still alive, so was this fear realistic or was it just a result of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some cases it was realistic fear. In other cases, it was just propaganda or the results thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you also looked into the problem of refugees; how many refugees there were, where there were most refugees. Did you look into that and do you know that 600.000 or 700.000 refugees remain in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did deal with the problem of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Do you know what happened in Zagreb after the killing of the entire Zec family? Was there a mass exodus of people from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know that there was a mass exodus of people from Zagreb. All I know about the event that you mentioned I know from the writing of the press and predominantly from what the Croatian press said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions about an event in Foca involving 40 Muslims. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: First of all, could you describe for the Tribunal the patch that was on the shoulder of -- I'm sorry. Could you please describe for us what you learned about these 40 Muslims when you were in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that these were people who had for the most part been in the leadership of the local branch of the Party of Democratic Action, or had links to the party, and that after Foca had fallen into the hands of the Serbs, the Serb forces, that they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: How did you learn this?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt this talking to the president of the municipality and president of the Crisis Staff, so-called Crisis Staff, of the Serbian municipality of Foca, as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Did you see anything in writing that contained any identifying information on these 40 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on the table of the president of the Crisis Staff a list of persons in alphabetical order with those 40 names on it, and he confirmed that these people on the list were indeed the people who were in custody in prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go back to your testimony about the Serb from the Serbian republic state security that you met in Bosnia. Could you describe for us the insignia that he had on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked to him, he was wearing civilian clothing, but from what he said, I learnt that he wore the uniform of AP Western Bosnia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: What is AP Western Bosnia, or what was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: AP means Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, and that was the territory under the control of Fikret Abdic in the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, around a town called Velika Kladusa mostly. And Fikret Abdic, as the accused said, closely cooperated both with the accused and with Radovan Karadzic, and he actively fought against the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Did this person tell you what he was there to do?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and his people, he said, had fought within the composition of a larger unit of armed forces of Western Bosnia in which there were quite a number of Muslims. And they were fighting against the 5th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, around Bihac. They were actually trying to take control of the town of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Did he tell you what eventually happened to those Muslim members of his unit?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was rather frustrated over it all, because after some sort of confidence was established between his own people and the Serbs, Abdic's people, that is to say the Muslims, one evening what happened was that a unit called the Panthers turned up. It was a special purposes unit within the forces of the Republika Srpska, and during that night they killed most of his men of ethnic -- of Muslim ethnicity. And he tried to complain about this, asked why it had happened, and the answer he was given, "Well, they're only Muslims." That was what he told me, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you give a written statement that you signed in the presence of an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And was that interview signed sometime in July of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And was this incident that you've just described with the Serb from the Republic of Serbia state security described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
