utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I can't remember whether that was mentioned, what I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's been a mistake here. As far as I remember, the witness said that that member of the DB was a member of the DB of Republika Srpska and not the Republic of Serbia. So Republika Srpska is an entity in itself, DB being state security. So it isn't the Republic of Serbia, it's Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. You've heard what Mr. Milosevic has asserted. Could you remind us, clarify what this man was a member of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a member of the state security of Republika Srpska. So not Republic of Serbia; that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McKeon, I'm not sure where we're going with this reference to the statement. We haven't had it exhibited and I don't think we want it exhibited now. The witness has given his evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions about your interviews of Mr. Seselj. I'd like to take you back to that. First of all, you said that Mr. Seselj was officially an opposition member. What did you mean by that statement?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant was that Mr. Seselj did not assume an official position in the power and authority of the Republic of Serbia, but informally, his power was there, his power was considerable. And de facto, in actual fact, he was part of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: How many times did you interview Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five to ten times. I can't remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And did you publish articles based on those interviews?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Seselj ever come to you after you published one of these articles to tell you that you had gotten something wrong?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Anastasijevic, were these interviews one-to-one interviews or was that like a press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly when I say it was an interview, they were interviews between myself and him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to ask a question about the statement because there was a suggestion made that his testimony about Mr. Seselj was a recent fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2000, did you put into your statement what you've testified to here today about Mr. Seselj claiming that Stanisic would call him up and ask to get 120 people together to go to Vukovar, for example? Did you have that in your written statement of the year 2000, summer of 2000?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Did you review your written statement before coming to testify here in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And is there anything in that statement that you saw was incorrect or, upon subsequent reflection testifying here today, you think is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the introduction of that statement now at this particular point in time would not be in order because the statement has so many things that were relevant for an examination but was not the topic of the examination-in-chief. And now in this re-direct, the Prosecution is going back to it. I don't think that that is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is on a very narrow topic alone, which is as to whether he's made up what he said about Seselj and the interview, and the Prosecution are entitled to rebut that suggestion by pointing out that there was a reference in a statement made in 2000, and on that narrow ground, they can refer to the statement, but not for anything else. Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: In the articles you published about the Seselj interview, did you make reference to this statement about Seselj being asked to provide men at the request of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about Vukovar, Ovcara, and the event at the hospital. I'd like to take you back to that, if I could, just for a moment. You were asked, first of all by amicus counsel, whether you learned this information from a high-ranking member of the JNA, and I believe you answered yes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court who that high-ranking member of the JNA is from whom you learned information about the involvement of the JNA in the Vukovar-Ovcara massacre.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Aleksandar Vasiljevic who, at the time we're talking about, was at the head of the second administration of the Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say this was known as KOS, the counter-intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: When you say at the time we're talking about, do you mean at the time of the events in Vukovar-Ovcara or at the time that you had a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time when the events in Ovcara came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was any reporting relationship between Mr. Vasiljevic and Major Sljivancanin at the time of the Vukovar-Ovcara events?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic told me that at the time these events took place, he was not in the environs of Vukovar himself and that it was later on that he learnt of the details. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: But my question is whether or not he told you that Major Sljivancanin, at the time of the events, somehow reported to him or worked for Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Vasiljevic having told me that Sljivancanin was under his direct command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And you mentioned a meeting that took place at the Velepromet before the prisoners taken from the hospital were murdered. Did you also learn that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He referred -- I don't think he referred to Velepromet. He simply referred to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Do you recall -- first of all, that meeting that you referred to, from whom did you learn about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also from General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And did he tell you where that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that it was held in the building that belonged to the company called Velepromet, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: When did you -- did you interview Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interviewed him together with other colleagues many times between 1994 and 1996. However, I have to point out that these were not classical interviews in the sense of everything being said there later published in the form of an interview in the newspaper concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: This information that you've provided the Tribunal this morning about what Mr. Vasiljevic told you about Vukovar-Ovcara, did you ever publish that information after your interview with Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was published several times in my texts and in the texts written by my colleagues who talked to the same source, and this was published in the magazine of Vreme. However, we did not mention our source in our articles. That is to say, we protected our source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that article was published?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several articles were published in 1994 and in 1995, and after that, usually on the anniversary of the events in Ovcara. So practically every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And just yes or no: Are those events also dealt with in the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in summer of 2000?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN ANASTASIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Anastasijevic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. The Chamber will now adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to take a seat. Yes. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put a sheet of paper with the personal details to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, on top of this sheet of paper, there is a number. That's the number you are referred to here in these proceedings, and without mentioning the names and dates that follow on this sheet, just answer my question with yes or no. On this sheet of paper there is a name, a birth date, a place of birth, and a family status written down. Does that refer to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the last line, in the last line, is this the post you held before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this sheet of paper needs to become an exhibit because it identifies the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness can give his -- or it can be given what he is to be called in these particular proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is C-1220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. And the Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be Prosecutor's Exhibit number 341.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you lived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Without referring to the -- your position, when did you stop working?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Sometime in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you stop working?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Because the process of production stopped completely in that area. I mean, the process of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the other employees, were there both Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Mostly Serbs. Almost all were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were they all laid off at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: They somewhat earlier. And I, according to a telegram, was supposed to be on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was an SDS party formed in your town?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was this done?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Sometime in 1990, 1991. I don't know. Something around there. 1990, beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you join this party?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you join the party? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The reason was that I heard Mr. Jovan Raskovic, and I realised that the Serb people have to go to elections on account of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did Mr. Jovan Raskovic say that you found so convincing that you joined the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood him, Croatia would have to have respect for the Serbs and that, in that way, the Serbs would exercise their rights in Croatia, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At that time, what was the atmosphere among the -- both people, Serbs and Croats, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: In principle, it was good, but as time went on, there was more and more fear and more and more tension.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did the Serbs fear?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: At all gatherings of the HDZ or any other ones, it was mainly bad messages that were sent to the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you -- what do you mean it was bad messages?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I remember, for example, even the top government officials in Croatia, for example Sime Djodan, when he said in the Easter message that Serbs were a disruptive factor and that they should be Catholicised, and there was more and more fear among the Serb people. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was a referendum held in your town at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: At one point in time, yes. I mean, the SAO Krajina should be established. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who organised this referendum?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the SDS. I mean, that's the way I think it was. From Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that the SAO was to be established. What was the exact question raised in the referendum? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I could not give the exact wording. It was something like secession from the Republic of Croatia. I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did this referendum take place?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: All of this was happening, I think, after what happened in parliament took place when some of the Serb MPs left parliament and never returned to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This referendum, did it have an effect on the daily life in your town?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Ordinary people thought it was some kind of protection and that -- and that something would be established that would protect us. Well, to put it simply, that the Croatian authorities would not come to that area. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your town is on the road -- belongs to the municipality of Ogulin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you should have a look at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. atlas to orient yourself. It's Exhibit 336. And if you look into the quarter D-2, you will find this town Ogulin. It's this orange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 19. Page 19, quarter D-2, and you find there an orange highlighted town, Ogulin. And going further down south-west, you come across the place the witness lived. And even further down that same road, you come across Saborsko. It's actually in already D-3. And when you go further down that same road, you come to Plitvice. This is the area we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let us first speak about the road to Ogulin where your town was situated at. Was this road accessible throughout the year 1991?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened that you couldn't access it any more?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, you see, sometime around the month of June, after those events Plitvice, some kind of line was established and all communication was disrupted in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who controlled the road then, the road between your town and Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know. What do you mean? What do you mean when?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said there was a line. Was it sort of a border?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, some kind of a natural border. This area over there was only populated by Serbs, and the other area was predominantly Croat. There was a mixed population. So there was this sort of natural border, and nobody communicated with anybody any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there actually a roadblock, and if so, who controlled the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: There were on both sides. At first there were some big rocks or some big pieces of wood on both sides. One on one side, the other on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who controlled these blockades?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, under the control of the Territorial Defence. Those were the very beginnings. There wasn't anything but the self-organised -- I mean, without weapons or, rather, with only hunting weapons. Those were the very beginnings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your town, was there a police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it a mixed police, Croats and Serbs, before the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Mixed, but there were more Serbs employed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croats leave, the Croat policemen, did they leave at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that and where did they go?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, they were there. One or two were from Saborsko, this neighbouring village, and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And did they go to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I think they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police at that time when the Croats left?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Father Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name? And maybe you'd speak a little bit louder.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Latas Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was he a local Serb?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did new policemen replace the Croats that had left?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those who came, the new policemen, which ethnicity did they have?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were they local Serbs or did they come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were they professional policemen, or what kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, they were not professionals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they get any training?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. A few younger men went for training to Knin and then they returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who trained -- do you know who trained them in Knin? Did they ever speak to you about it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know who trained them. I just know that they went for some training there and returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many new policemen came and were trained in Knin?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Approximately -- well, I don't know exactly, but a few of them would go and then a few groups too, perhaps five or six from a certain place, and several such groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, they wore some camouflage uniforms, but they were predominantly blue as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they have badges on these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I think the emblems were of the police of the SAO Krajina. I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did these -- what kind of weapons did these policemen have?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, they had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mean automatic rifles? Did you hear my question? I asked you whether they were automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether they got these weapons in your town or in Knin?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: At that time, those were the very beginnings, we did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This police force, these new policemen, did they have a particular name for their unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: They were usually called Martic's Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a person with the name Medakovic

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: When a municipality was established again there in my town when we were separated from the municipality of Ogulin, he was the first president Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the municipality, and he was also the commander of these police called Martic's Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a professional policeman or what kind of a job did he have?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No. He was a student, but I don't think that he graduated at all. He was a student.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So he was a local person, then? You knew him from before?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a person Djuro Ogrizovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: He was from a place about five or six kilometres away from the place where I was, but before the war he did not live there. He lived somewhere around Celine. I personally did not know him from before. I knew him sort of just like this, but I knew who he was and where he was from, but I was never actually introduced, we never actually met.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said he did not -- he did not live there. Where did he live before the war? Where did he --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Before the war, he lived in Zrenjanin -- no, Vrsac. In Vrsac. But his house was in this neighbouring village, his parents' house where he was born. That's where he came during the summer, but that's not where he lived all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Vrsac, is that in Croatia or where?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What position, if any, did he have in your town when the war started? Or in summer, let's say in summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. He was with Martic's men. He was old. Well, sort of old. He had the rank of a colonel. Now, how this happened, I don't know. Some people said that he conferred it upon himself. He retired, but he was some kind of an inspector or something in the police force. I don't know which rank he actually had, but he did bear the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where would you see him in town?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I saw him in passing. This is a small town. It's not a big town, and everybody sees everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Only later, when the war had already started.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did you -- where did you meet him then and what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: This was already later, much later, when the war was already in full swing. I don't know. Perhaps this was already 1993. 1992 or 1993. Often I saw him at barracks at the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These barracks and command of the brigade, was it in your town, in the town centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in the centre of this town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ogrizovic, did he go to the brigade headquarters? Did you -- did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was there often, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whom he met there when he went there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, for the most part -- well --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question. I had asked you when you saw him, do you know whom he met there, to whom -- what he was doing in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, he had dealings with these top people, senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "senior officers," army officers or police officers? Whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Army. Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that you spoke to him on one occasion, either in 1992 or 1993. What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I mean when I said that, actually there was this quarrel between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you quarrel about?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, he said that I was supposed to do a lot more because I held such a position. This was a big transport company and that I was supposed to do a lot more, and that made no sense whatsoever. And -- I mean, he was the only person who could think something like that. And in this way, he really wanted to provoke me. He made a few mistakes. I mean, he made -- he did a few things that were not really very good, and he did this at a Serb place -- of course, I did not know about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's difficult to see where we're going with this, and there seems to be a lot of detail that isn't going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a little bit difficult. I want to work with this witness to work out the role of this Ogrizovic in relation to the police and what he did. And what he actually did, the witness tries to avoid to say where he was working and to actually explain what this person did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he won't give the evidence, he won't give it, but -- very well. Perhaps he doesn't know. Can you help us as to what this person did or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. Why not? He was in charge of this group of Martic's men. And in my opinion, in my opinion, the main thing he did was looting. But, for example, when somebody would come, it were as if he were some kind of an intelligence officer there in the area. When somebody would come, for example, from Rijeka via Hungary and Serbia to see us, he sort of interrogated these people. I think he's the one who actually took this upon himself. I mean, I don't really know how to express myself the right way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said he did wrong things. Did you discuss what he did wrong with him on this one occasion? Did you accuse him of having done something?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I did. Well, had I known then at the time, then I would have. He mined the railway and also the electric pylons in a Serb place so that we were left without power for a while. And there were some other things. He never did it in a way where he could show his courage outside of the area controlled by Serbs. He had no courage to go to Ogulin or further away and do it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So -- wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: And this is why we had to pay the price later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he mined the railway and also an electric pole. He did that in Serb regions?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's where the problem lies, because he did it in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did he do that? Was it before the war started?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Before. In the very beginning. He mined the railway line in a Serb place where there's only a school train going and carrying children of Serb origin. And had I known -- I was interrogated by the then-authorities about that. They wanted to see whether I knew of this. And had I known it at the time, I would have told them, but I learned of it later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when -- when he mined the electrical facility, what did it cause for the region?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, from Ogulin until our area in Saborsko, we all have the same line, and he was in this hamlet in our area. So they did this to the detriment of Saborsko. And then we had no power. We had no power after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were the Croats blamed for this mining? You said you didn't know that it was him at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who was, but there was an investigation launched in that area, our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you confronted him on these matters when you met him in the headquarters, how did he react to this? Did he deny having done it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Then a very big argument broke out between us because for these very ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you mobilised into the Serb TO at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in July or August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you get a call-up letter, and if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: From the TO who -- which organised it. It was from the command of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it -- was it a general mobilisation for all the men in your town?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the TO commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Nikola Dokmanovic. I think he had a rank of major. He had graduated from the academy and then he worked in the municipality in the national defence office, and he was not in the army any more. He had graduated from a military academy and then was in the JNA, and then after that, due to family reasons, he transferred to the municipality, to the national defence office there in the municipality. So when in my place a municipality was established, he was at the helm of national defence as the most capable person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you were mobilised, did you get a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you get this weapon?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: We got weapons from the army. The army armed that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say the army, is that JNA or which army do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, no. At the time when this was happening with the TO, these were the very beginnings. So we had no weapons at the time. But there was a factory there which had some weapons, rifles, you know, for their own protection, and that was taken from them. And also hunting rifles were collected. Just any kind of weapons that were there. And that was in the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you later on get proper weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who provided these weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The army would bring in weapons at night and then overnight it would be distributed, and that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "the army," whom do you mean? Which army?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The JNA. That's who I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did these weapons arrive? Were they loose or were they in boxes?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: It was in crates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was anything written on the crates?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, they were just regular crates and, yes, there was some marks on it, say 48. That's the type of the rifle. I can't remember all of the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did they do with the crates?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Once the weapons were distributed, we set the crates on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, we were told to burn the crates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who told you to burn the crates?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, the command. The army, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that you received the weapons at night. At what time? I mean not the exact hour, in which time period did you receive such weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Usually after dark. Once it became dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And which ones?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Early 1991. I think it was then or around there. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, not in the first half. No, it wasn't in the first half. It could have been September, October, then, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also receive uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Afterwards, when the uniforms came in from somewhere, I guess from some warehouses, then we were given uniforms later on, but not in the beginning. We first received weapons and then uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who provided the uniforms; the local people or again the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a uniform from the JNA. I don't know where it came from, but there was a warehouse in my place, and then also in the vicinity of my place there was also a JNA warehouse there with a large number of uniforms there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did JNA officers arrive in the town later on?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did they arrive and who arrived?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't give you the date. I know it was late autumn, maybe October or November. As far as I can remember, 18 officers of the JNA came on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think they came from Belgrade or somewhere there. That's what we were told, at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know from which corps, from which army corps they came?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When these officers arrived, did they -- did they change anything in the TO?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. After all, it was a more structured command. The discipline was better. They raised the level of discipline, and it was along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was a brigade formed after they arrived?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. They simply took over the TO command, the command of that brigade that was self-organised under the TO. They simply improved it in a professional sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did this brigade have a name?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think so but I can't remember any more. I think it was 124th Light Infantry, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: You mean then?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: When these people came? Petar Trbovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a professional JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that there was a headquarters in the centre of your town. Was it actually -- was this the headquarters of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was it in a military facility from before the war, or where was the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Before the war, in my place there was a military barracks, and it was there that the command of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many battalions did the brigade have?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which battalion were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I was in the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Grba, Bogdan. In the beginning he was offered that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No. He was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to discuss with the witness a military map. And, Your Honours, you have this map in your binder. It's tab 9 in the Exhibit 326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's not. Let it be formally exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 326, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this map, did you have time to study this map after your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, look at the map. Look also on top of the map, what is written on top of the map, and please study the legend. It is a map referring to the attack on Saborsko. It's a military map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your information, this map was provided by the Croatian government, and we will refer to the authenticity, we will provide additional information on this matter in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just wonder if this witness, since he doesn't seem to be familiar with it, is the best witness to produce it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this witness is very excited. This is at least the impression I got from him. So I would like to repeat the questions now that he had looked at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because I think he's very excited and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, look at the map. And did you see -- did you discuss this map, when you came to The Hague, with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see this sort of map, did you see this sort of map during the events?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You, in your -- and would you, in your position as you had at that time, would you handle such maps, or who would handle them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not an officer at all. I don't hold a rank, so these abbreviations and terminologies are not something that I know. I am an ordinary soldier. So I wasn't able to participate in creation of this map, nor did anyone ever ask me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These maps are handled by officers and not by the soldiers themselves; is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: What I mean is that this plan of attack, nobody asked me regarding this anything, nor do I know anything. Well, how could they ask me this? Professional people developed this. I never saw this before. This is the first time I see this map with this -- with these markings. I saw maps before but without these markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we just want to discuss a few matters on the map with you. You do not need to know the details, and there is no indication that you made the map or were involved in it. Where was -- when you look at the map, where was the head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness explained several times already that he had nothing to do with this map. There is no reason to go into details. There is no sense in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Milosevic. We're with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know anything about it. He can't help us. Now, it may be better if you ask him if he can give some evidence about the events. It may be better if we lay the ground in that way, and then it may be possible for him to refer to the map, but he can't produce it for the reasons the accused rightly gives; he doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason why I used this map with the witness is actually the reason -- this is the best map of the area, the most detailed map, and actually, when we come to the details, what was where and which unit was where, he is well able to explain it. This is the reason why I introduced the map, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe. But the way he's giving his evidence, let him give his account and then we'll come back to the map if it's possible, but at the moment it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can put the -- for the time being, we can put this map away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that Mr. Trbovic was the commander of the brigade. Do you know to whom he was subordinated?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think that the next area of military formation was Korenica. They had a division there. And then Knin was above.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know where the headquarters of the Korenica division, as you say, where it was situated?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think it was in Mukinje, on Plitvice Lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how do you know that? What information did you get to this effect?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I have no information. It was just known that it was up there. Division, the command that was in charge of the brigade. Everybody knew this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know the name of the commander in Mukinje?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I knew the name of the commander, but right now I can't remember. It won't come to me right now. I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a military headquarters also in Slunj or near Slunj?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, there was a military exercise area between my place and Slunj, and it belonged to the former times when we had Croatia there. And there was a large military formation stationed there. And that's in the area between my place and Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how far is it away from -- this military facility, how far is it away from Saborsko? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Which one do you have in mind? You mean the training area?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, the training area, this exercise area, well, it's hard for me to say now. It's not far. Perhaps ten kilometres from Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Through the woods. And if you took the road, it would take longer. But if you took a shortcut through the woods, it would be about ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was the military commander of this place, this military training place?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The commander of the training area was -- I don't know. He was called Ledeni, which means "frozen," and held the rank of general. I think it was the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Cedomir Bulat?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, but I know of him. He was a colonel, and in his staff he was one of the leading senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: But for a while in the beginning, Stipetic was commander, General Stipetic, in Slunj, in the training area, in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's speak about Cedomir Bulat. Did he come to your town and meet the military staff there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. He used to come and meet people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he meet with Trbovic, the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't see that. But I'm sure that he did meet him, because he went to the command, and who else was he going to meet there; the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he the superior of Trbovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No. I don't know that they had a -- that there was a hierarchical link between them. They both had the same rank. So I don't think that one was subordinate to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the JNA officers arrived, did the TO also receive different weapons, artillery weapons? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did they receive?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think mortars, smaller and larger ones, 170 millimetres or 105 millimetres, I don't know, but thereabout. Those types of mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the local TO members operate such weapons or did JNA soldiers operate such weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, the TO was trained. These officers who knew this trained others, and there were people there who served in that branch of service when they were in the army. So they knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go briefly into private session just to explain the role that the witness had in his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because it's quite identifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the beginning of your testimony, we spoke about where Saborsko was situated, that is on the road to Plitvice. Could the people from your town travel on this road to Plitvice freely or was it blocked at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Up until the first conflicts - how can I put this? - communications were normal. But after the events had started, you couldn't go along that way any more because, quite simply, communications were severed. You couldn't move along that road any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Saborsko, is that a Croatian village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a police station in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Not before the war, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during the war? In November, for instance, in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, that's -- let me see. November 1991. No. November 1991. Well, I don't know. I don't know about that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were Croatian soldiers in the village before it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: It was rumoured that there were Croatian soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, that is what was rumoured. And they said that Saborsko was a stronghold. That was the information that was coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But who said that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, who. The officers there in their normal communication amongst themselves. Now, whether they did or didn't have proper information about that, I don't know, but those were the kind of stories going round.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Saborsko attacked, and did you participate in this attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was it attacked?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think it was in November 1991, thereabouts. At least in the first half of November, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before this attack occurred, when did you learn that it would happen? Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, in the evening, the commander of the battalion said, "We're going to Saborsko tomorrow, and the following will be going: You, you, you, and you." Because we were just attached to -- as reinforcements with all the technical staff and equipment that was already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before you were told that you had to participate, did you see troop movements? Before that evening.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. You could see tanks coming in. There were several tanks. APCs, armoured personnel carriers; they were on the move.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see General -- sorry. Did you see Cedomir Bulat in your town before the attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He passed that way. You could see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you go for the attack? Was there a gathering place?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, a small village nearby. Its name is Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you arrive with a group of people from your unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. There were about 20 to 30 of us in that group, in my group, the one I was in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you arrive there? Was it in the morning or the evening?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, it's not far from my village. About eight or nine kilometres away. So it doesn't take long when you're in a car, in a vehicle. So it was in the morning the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, how many soldiers did you see, approximately?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. Several hundred, I would say, but again I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those soldiers that you saw, were they all from the local TO or were they others as well? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The army and those of us added to it who were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "the army," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those JNA soldiers, were they conscripts, do you know? Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I didn't talk to them. As I say, I had my assignment. Everybody was deployed and given an assignment of his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see policemen also at this gathering place, Licka Jesenica?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The police were there, but I didn't see them because they were sort of on the other side. Yes. You mean the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned several of the commanders of the Martic police, and you mentioned Djuro Ogrizovic. Was he there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, he was there. I didn't see him, but quite certainly he was there. Because as I say, those policemen there from the other side, they had -- I don't know how to explain this to you. I learnt that here about this other business.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Bulat?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What -- when did he come and what did he do?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I think that he commanded the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, because he was leading the operation. He was in command with that training facility and all the people that had come in, and he led the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he address the soldiers, including you, at Licka Jesenica?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, you see, we came to Licka Jesenica sometime during the morning. We were there all day and all night. It was very cold, and we had to be there among the houses. We were pretty nervous by that time, and people didn't like having to be there. And in the morning, I know that he lined all the soldiers up and explained what they were waiting for, that it was bad weather, in fact, that the weather conditions were bad and that the planes could not fly. Along those lines, that's what he said, and that we'd have to wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you what the purpose of this attack was, why Saborsko was attacked?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Saborsko is a place, and my own village was under siege. It was surrounded on all sides. You couldn't get out from any side. So it was in a complete encirclement, completely under siege. I don't know. I didn't take part in the life of Licka, but I did hear that the leadership was on the move towards Saborsko and that they wanted to have the roads opened, that the communication lines should be open and that not a hair of anybody's head should be harmed. But these things weren't enforced in Saborsko. You couldn't get in and you couldn't get out. And Cedo explained this in that way, that it had to fall in order to be able to link up the Serb lands and get out from that place because you couldn't get away from there. It was in an encirclement. And there were shortages of everything; salt, fuel. No strategic fuel of any kind. Shortages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you -- can you describe to us how Saborsko was attacked? What happened first? You have already mentioned aeroplanes. Was it attacked by air?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. The planes attacked from the air. That's clear. And of course there was the artillery. They went first. And then the infantry attack came next.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The artillery, where was it positioned? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: The artillery was up along those hills, and they were the ones that were able to launch the operation. There were just several tanks that opened fire on this Saborsko area, but all the others were positioned on the elevations round about, and that's where they could act from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's now 12.15, so it may be convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1220, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. During the adjournment and any others there may be during your evidence, please don't speak to anybody about it. Don't let anyone else speak to you about it until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be permitted to make a short observation in relation to the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Higgins. We've had some correspondence about your position, but we shall allow you to make the submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. It's a very short submission just to say that the evidence so far has been led to some extent by my learned friend, and it's perhaps important that in relation to the remaining evidence concerning the attack on Saborsko, that it is the witness who gives the evidence in response to non-leading questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will have that in mind. I think it's slightly harsh criticism, but let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you had described that there was -- that there was artillery in the hills. Do you know who operated this artillery, which units?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I think it was that mortar unit, the one 120-millimetre one, and I suppose the 82-millimetre one. And on the training facility, there were 130-millimetre ones. I don't know, are they guns, cannons? Whatever. And their range, they have their range. And there were several tanks there too. They were active as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you speak about the training facility, do you mean this JNA training facility that you mentioned before near Slunj, or is --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. That's the one. From that area. So I suppose they are long-range weapons that can operate from that distance and that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have already mentioned the infantry. From when did they get engaged and from which direction did they approach Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, please, how do you mean which direction? What do you mean and when? Could you clarify that question, please, what you mean by it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did the infantry attack, and from which direction did they attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to be able to tell you that now, but after the artillery opened fire, then the infantry came in after that. From a number of directions and axes. They came to Saborsko from several directions. All I can tell you is in the direction I came from and engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which direction did you come from?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to explain. There's that road there, and it curves, and we took a shortcut through some woods and some thickets, and we came out onto Semnicka road, which was a dead end. It ended in the forest. It was a big forest and the road didn't go any further than that. So they were conifers, that kind of forest. And the group I was in, we had to cut across there. Not follow the road but to cut across, take a cut and come onto this Sumska road in the forest and take up our positions there and see that nobody appear from the forest. So that was my task, the one I was engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that actually before Saborsko, in the direction of your town?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, looking at it from my direction, it is before Saborsko but to the east of Saborsko. So it is from that area there where I was stationed and my group. You can't see Saborsko from there at all. All you can see is two little hamlets. Their names are Tuk, that's one, and the other one is Solaje. Those two little villages. Just a few houses, hamlets, actually. Tuk also is composed of just a few houses, and so is Solaje, several Serb houses there. And Dumencici, another small -- another hamlet, several houses only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What exactly was your task in that place that you reached? What did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't quite clear on what we were supposed to do. This Sumska road that was a dead end, that didn't lead anywhere, just served as a way out of the forest, we were to stop there and see that nobody came from the forest. The enemy, the Croatian army, in fact. That was our task and assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your unit, did you actually get engaged in fighting with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Saborsko put up resistance? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No. I don't think it did, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was any Serb soldier killed during this operation?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was anyone wounded?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: One person was seriously wounded - he lost an eye from a mine - and another one was just slightly grazed. Just a slight injury there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did this incident with the mine happen? Was it on -- when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, when he was passing by that way, he came across a mine that had been placed there by the infantry. Now, when the mine had been laid there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you were in this place, in this place where you were -- where your unit was sent to, you said you could see these three villages, Tuk, Dumencici and Solaje. When did you see in these villages?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I saw them -- actually, it's only those three hamlets that you can see from the position I was in. You can't see any of the rest of Saborsko from the forest. So when they came in, they were small houses, mostly wooden houses, and they were set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who set fire to them? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I didn't, but the soldiers that were moving along that way, whether it was the army or the Territorial Defence or whoever. The Serb forces, whichever they were, they set fire to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually see them setting fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No. And I couldn't because we just saw that the houses were burning. Now, who had set fire to them, we -- I don't know. We couldn't see that. It was quite a long way away. You couldn't recognise anybody from that distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You just said you couldn't recognise anybody from that distance. Did you see people setting fire on the houses that you did not recognise?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. I saw people, but I couldn't recognise them, see who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did they put fire to the houses? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, when they entered the village, they set fire to it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in this position, did you see any higher ranking officer?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Not there, no. At least, from where I was standing I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in this position, did you have radio contact? Did you have any communication, not you personally but the unit, with others?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had a radio transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to whom did you have contact? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, with the command, those who were in command. He was sort of a leader for our group. He communicated with them, and I know that he said that it was our task to stay there in that position until the order for withdrawal came, and we spent the whole time there at that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you withdraw and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: It was night-time already. We had withdrawn to the centre of Saborsko and went to the houses after that from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you reached Saborsko, in which state was the village? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Everything was set on fire, was burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see who did that, who set the houses on fire, or were they already burning when you came?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: They were already burning, all of them, when we came.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the public buildings in Saborsko? Were they also set on fire?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Right there, there's only the school building, and that hadn't been set on fire yet while I was there. And there was a shop inside or, rather, a makeshift shop in a room of the school building. You know, it's a very small place, so this was just a small sort of shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does Saborsko have a church?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened to the church?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: The church was still standing. Nothing had happened to it. Perhaps it was hit with a projectile of some sort, but it hadn't been destroyed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say "at the time." Was it destroyed later on?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, it was, later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was it destroyed and when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: When it happened, I do not know, but it must have been a fortnight later or a month later when it was mined.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived in Saborsko, were there many soldiers there? Whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers. All of them were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any police staff present?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were some policemen there too. The police had come out there from all sides. They'd all come down into the centre and then they were all sent back. There was no command there at all any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you -- when you arrived there, what did the soldiers and the police do? What did you see them do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, as I've just told you, the whole -- it was already night-time. Everybody was gathered there. All I can say is that I saw them start looting. Several of them, they started looting that shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who did that? What kind of persons did that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Several people. Two or three of them. It was only them that could have taken it into their heads to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "them"? You said it could only be them who --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, those -- how can I put this? The people that suddenly took it into their heads to start looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, you've said there were police and soldiers. Now, was there anybody else in the village? Can you just give us a short answer, please? Who was it who was looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be about two or three people from the so-called Martic police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any Croats when you were in Saborsko at that evening?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: I saw a few people, very old. Just a few very old people as they were passing by.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies, dead, dead people?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No. No, none.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in this Saborsko and saw the burning houses, how did you feel? What impression did it make on you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Oh, terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, I can. I had never seen any such thing in all my life, so it was a terrible thing for me to see. There were people who were around me who were sort of laughing, and I said, "That is pitiful. And if this ever happens to us, you're going to see it's going to be even worse." It just crossed my mind then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who were laughing? What people were laughing; soldiers, policemen, or others? Who?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Well, they the soldiers. Well, look, I mean, there were so many people I don't know. There was such a lot of commotion there. There were people there that I had never seen in my life or people who I did not know at all. I mean, I cannot know everybody or, rather, I cannot know every single person from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any commanders there, higher-ranking soldiers such as your battalion commander or even his superiors, in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Yes. His superiors, yes, but I did not see him. I saw him only when we returned to that neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who is "him"? You said "him." "I did not see him. I saw him only when we returned to the neighbouring village." And who is "him"?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Commander of the battalion. The commander of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's Mr. Trbovic.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who, then? I mean, can you tell us the name?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1220
utterances.text: Grba Cedo Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Bulat in Saborsko?
